blocks.text: …make people disappear on paper. I changed my mind. Please. I want to go home."
I didn't call the number on the paperwork. I called 911, and then I wrapped her in a heated blanket from the supply closet and sat with her on the floor until the ambulance came.

Her name was Rachel. She was thirty-four, a mother of two from Columbus, and she'd been reported missing four days earlier. She'd been drowning in gambling debts that her husband didn't know about, more than $200,000 owed to people who'd started making threats. A man she met online promised he could make her "start over." For $15,000, his group would fake her death: a death certificate signed by a doctor who'd lost his license, a "body" received by a cooperating funeral home, a quick cremation of an empty box.
To make the transport look real, they sedated her with a mild medication and zipped her into the bag. The bracelet was pre-dated for the day the paperwork would be filed.
But she woke up early in the van. She'd already been having second thoughts. Lying in the dark, thinking about her kids, she knew she couldn't do it.

My supervisor, Mr. Hollis, had been paid by the group to sign receipts and run the crematorium for "special deliveries." That's why he'd told me not to call the police until morning. He planned to come in early and handle it himself.
Investigators found eleven other fake deaths processed through our funeral home in two years. Every one of those people was alive. Most had disappeared willingly to escape debts or legal trouble.
A few were trying to escape abusive partners. The group's doctor, the driver, and Mr. Hollis were arrested within a week.
Rachel went home to her husband and children. She told him everything, including the debts. He was devastated, but he stayed. She's in a recovery program for gambling addiction now.
She sent me a card in the spring. Inside was a drawing by her six-year-old daughter: a stick figure with a blanket and the words "Thank you for opening the bag."
I still work nights. At a different funeral home.
If gambling is affecting you or someone you love, the National Problem Gambling Helpline is available 24/7 at 1-800-522-4700.
